Compile files and executable projects with the released compiler.

The release compiler directly emits supported programs. It does not invoke a C++
compiler, host C compiler, assembler, or linker.

## Compile a source file

```bash
hy check hello.hy
hy compile hello.hy -o hello
chmod +x hello
./hello
```

The default output is a standalone Linux x86-64 ELF executable. `check` finds
syntax and type errors; `compile` is the final authority because it also rejects
features the current backend cannot emit.

## Build a project

```bash
hy build app/App.hyproj -o app/bin/app
chmod +x app/bin/app
./app/bin/app
```

Executable project references contribute source files to one native compilation.
The current release also builds `efi`, `kernel`, and `os` manifests; see
[Projects and references](/tools/projects/). It does not produce library archives,
build workspaces, resolve packages, or run tests for you.

## Rebuild the compiler

Contributors can use a verified release binary as a seed to rebuild the compiler's
Hydrogen project closure. This is Hydrogen-only; a clean source-only checkout still
needs a trusted initial seed.

```bash
hy check hello.hy

chmod +x hello
./hello Hydrogen
```

For an executable project:

```bash
hy build app/App.hyproj -o app/bin/app
```

Project references supply source to one combined executable. `efi` and `kernel`
manifests emit PE32+ images, while an `os` manifest builds its referenced images
into an output directory. The CLI does not produce standalone library archives.

## Diagnostics and IR

```bash
hy check hello.hy --emit-ir
```

`check --emit-ir` prints bound executable IR for inspection; it does not create a
runnable debug executable. Failed `compile` and `build` commands return non-zero
and preserve an existing output artifact.

## UEFI output

```bash
hy compile uefi_hello.hy --target uefi-x64 -o BOOTX64.EFI
file BOOTX64.EFI
```

`BOOTX64.EFI` is firmware code, not a Linux executable. Put it on a FAT EFI
system partition or use the Australis ISO workflow, then boot it with UEFI
firmware or QEMU/OVMF.

The supported language surface and output targets in the current release.

This guide describes the published [Hydrogen `alpha-0.0.2`](https://github.com/Aurora-Softwares/Hylang-Compiler/releases/tag/alpha-0.0.2) release.
Hydrogen releases ship the self-hosted Hydrogen compiler. This is the compiler you
use to write programs and build Linux-native applications. The current Australis
OS tree requires a newer development compiler checkout for raw `AUKR` kernels
and AUEX `.exec` applications.

The current release runs on Linux x86-64. Its default output is a standalone Linux
x86-64 executable. It can also emit PE32+ `uefi-x64` firmware images for a
constrained bootloader and early kernel sequence. Windows and macOS host
executables are future ports.

## Supported language surface

| Area | Available now |
| --- | --- |
| Program structure | Namespaces, classes, structs, interfaces, access modifiers, static and instance members |
| Values | Signed and unsigned integral widths, `bool`, strings, arrays, enums, and `var` |
| Control flow | `if`, `while`, `for`, `break`, `continue`, and `return` |
| Objects | Constructors, inheritance, virtual dispatch, interface calls, overloads, static fields, and recursion |
| Linux services | Console output, file text/bytes, integer parsing, and managed allocation/GC |
| Projects | Executable, EFI, kernel, and OS `.hyproj` projects with source references |
| UEFI | Literal console output, screen clearing, key wait, image launch, boot-services exit, and a fixed early-kernel initialization sequence |

Generics, exceptions, a general pointer/foreign-function model, a package manager,
and an interpreter are still outside this release. See the language pages for
examples of the supported subset.

## Targets

```bash
# Linux-native executable
hy compile hello.hy -o hello

# UEFI application
hy compile hello.hy --target uefi-x64 -o BOOTX64.EFI
```

`uefi-x64` has a restricted entry-point profile rather than the Linux runtime.
It supports the built-in `System.Uefi` and `System.Kernel` calls documented in
[Builtin APIs](/runtime/builtins/), but not arbitrary methods, file I/O, or a
general-purpose UEFI library.

## One-line installers for the next preview

The website now serves the installer scripts below. They require a newer,
manifest-bearing GitHub release asset. The current `alpha-0.0.2` release does
not contain those assets, so the scripts will report that no compatible release
is available until the next preview is published.

Linux x86-64:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://hylang.co.uk/install.sh | HYDROGEN_CHANNEL=alpha bash
```

Windows x64 PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:HYDROGEN_CHANNEL='alpha'; irm https://hylang.co.uk/install.ps1 | iex
```

Both scripts download an official release archive, verify the release digest
and SHA-256 sidecar, then install to a user-owned directory. The Linux script
creates `~/.local/bin/hy`; add that directory to `PATH` if necessary. The
Windows script adds the new `bin` directory to the user `PATH` for new
terminals. Stable-channel installers omit the `HYDROGEN_CHANNEL` setting once
a stable release exists. Native update and uninstall commands for these new
assets are still in development.

Firmware console and image launch

Section titled “Firmware console and image launch”

The bootloader entry point can clear the console before output, wait for a key after output, and start one EFI image from the same boot volume:

Early kernel sequence

Section titled “Early kernel sequence”

A separately compiled kernel EFI image can leave boot services and use early physical-memory, virtual-memory, heap, and framebuffer operations. These calls must appear in the supported order:

ExitBootServices() captures the final UEFI memory map and retries with a fresh map key when needed. The kernel then reserves conventional memory, installs its own four-level page tables, and can display printable ASCII through a supported 32-bit RGB or BGR GOP framebuffer. The early heap is a zero-filled, 16-byte aligned bump allocator; it does not free allocations. Optional System.Kernel.Memory.AllocatePage() calls go after ApplyPolicy() and before Heap.Initialize(). Optional System.Kernel.Heap.Allocate(<literal>) calls go after Heap.Initialize() and accept literal sizes from 1 byte through 1 MiB.

This path does not provide general object allocation, files, an ordinary keyboard API, or arbitrary calls after the handoff. A bootloader that calls StartImage() cannot also call ExitBootServices().

Native generations, UEFI proof output, and bootstrap boundaries.

> This is contributor documentation. Release users install `hy` and
> do not need the historical C++ bootstrap to use Hydrogen.

The Hydrogen-written compiler emits standalone Linux x86-64 ELF executables by
default. It binds the complete source/reference closure of its CLI project and can
compile itself. It can additionally produce constrained PE32+ UEFI bootloader
and early-kernel images.

## UEFI target

The `uefi-x64` path is implemented in Hydrogen. It writes a minimal PE32+ EFI
image, provides an x86-64 EFI entry stub, encodes console text as UTF-16, and
calls firmware protocols through the UEFI system table. `mtools` and `xorriso`
can package the executable into boot media; they do not compile it.

This is intentionally not a general ABI/runtime layer. It lowers a fixed set of
static-entry operations: literal console output, screen clearing, key wait, image
launch, and early-kernel handoff. The kernel path captures the final memory map,
exits boot services, installs owned page tables, and can use a basic heap and GOP
framebuffer console. Arbitrary method bodies, general firmware wrappers, and
foreign-function calls remain future work.

"$HYDROGEN" build samples/self_hosting/Hydrogen.Compiler.Cli/Hydrogen.Compiler.Cli.hyproj \

chmod +x hydrogen-rebuilt

## The current milestone

The released compiler runs on Linux x86-64 and directly emits standalone Linux
x86-64 executables. Its `uefi-x64` target can create bootloader and early-kernel
images, including a constrained transition out of UEFI boot services and direct
framebuffer text. This is still a fixed compilation profile rather than a complete
UEFI library or a general operating-system kernel.

Australis OS and native Australis applications are the primary direction. Linux
is the development host today; Windows and macOS compiler ports will follow when
they can be properly packaged and validated.

## Current Australis development

The compiler source checkout used by Australis builds a separate raw `AUKR`
kernel image and checked AUEX `.exec` applications. Australis also loads small
AUN1 machine-code programs in hardware ring 3; the Hydrogen compiler does not
yet emit that native format. These capabilities are newer than the documented
`alpha-0.0.2` release. See [Projects and references](/tools/projects/) and
[Australis applications](/tools/australis-applications/) for the development workflow.
Control visibility with public and private members.

The released compiler supports public, private, and protected members.

Modifier Visibility
public Visible everywhere in the compilation
private Restricted to the declaring class
protected Available to the declaring class and derived classes

Classes may inherit from a base class. Static methods and fields belong to the class rather than an instance.
Allocate, index, and share managed arrays.

The released compiler supports managed arrays of its supported element types.

Array counts must be int; void[] is invalid. Elements are zero/default initialized. Arrays are mutable reference types, so assignment and passing to a method retain the same underlying array. Out-of-range access is a runtime error.

Arrays may contain primitive values, strings, enums, structs, and class references:

The current release has no built-in List<T>, map, set, or generic collection. Use arrays and explicit counters until the standard library provides them.
Branch, loop, continue, break, and return from Hydrogen methods.

The released compiler supports if, while, for, break, continue, and return.

Use for when initialization, condition, and update belong together:

return; exits a void method. return expression; supplies a value from a non-void method. Exceptions are not part of the current release; use a status value or explicit condition for recoverable errors.

Enums are declared alongside classes at namespace scope:

Members without an explicit value begin at zero and increase by one. Enums can be fields, locals, parameters, return values, and array elements. Compare members of the same enum with == or !=. Console output formats an enum numerically, so select a string explicitly when human-readable output matters.
Use classes, fields, constructors, instance methods, and recursion.

Methods belong to classes or structs. The released compiler supports static and instance methods, constructors, fields, parameters, return values, overloads, inheritance, interfaces, virtual dispatch, and recursion.

new Counter(10) allocates a managed reference object and invokes its constructor. Field initializers run before the constructor body. A class without a declared constructor has a parameterless default constructor. Fields start at zero, false, or null when not initialized.

Class assignment copies a reference, not an object. this refers to the current instance. Static methods have no this; pass an object explicitly to access its instance members.

An overload can use the same name with different parameter types. Derived classes can call base constructors and use inherited members; interface calls dispatch to the implementing class or struct. Struct assignment copies the value, while class assignment copies a reference. Static fields are shared by the class. Generic methods are not part of this release.
Arithmetic, comparison, logical, unary, and string operators.

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` | Arithmetic; `+` also concatenates strings |
| `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | Comparison |
| `&&`, `\|\|`, `!` | Logical AND, OR, and NOT |
| `-value` | Unary numeric negation |

```csharp
int remainder = 10 % 3;
bool inRange = remainder > 0 && remainder < 100;
string message = "Count: " + remainder;
```

`&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right-hand side is evaluated only when needed.

instead.

Organize Hydrogen programs with namespaces, classes, and an entry point.

Hydrogen programs contain namespaces and types; executable statements belong inside methods. There are no top-level statements or free functions.

Namespaces use braces. A source can also declare a class in the global namespace.

Imports

Section titled “Imports”

Place imports before declarations. They let a file use simple names for types in that namespace but do not leak to other files. Use fully qualified builtin names, such as System.Console.WriteLine; this is the stable spelling recognized by the released compiler.

Entry point

Section titled “Entry point”

The released compiler accepts static Main methods returning void or int, with either no parameters or one string[] parameter. Project source files are listed in a .hyproj manifest; namespaces do not require a directory layout.
Core values, strings, arrays, null, and local type inference.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `sbyte`, `byte` | Signed and unsigned 8-bit integers |
| `short`, `ushort` | Signed and unsigned 16-bit integers |
| `int`, `uint` | Signed and unsigned 32-bit integers |
| `long`, `ulong` | Signed and unsigned 64-bit integers |
| `nint`, `nuint` | Signed and unsigned native-size integers (64-bit on the current target) |
| `byte` | Unsigned byte, useful for file contents |
| `bool` | `true` or `false` |
| `string` | Immutable managed byte string |
| `void` | A method returns no value |
| `T[]` | Mutable managed array |

Class instances are reference values; structs have value semantics. `null` is
assignable to strings, classes, and arrays. Accessing a null receiver is a runtime
error. Enums provide named numeric constants. Floating-point values are not in
this release.

## Strings

```csharp
string message = "Count: " + 42 + ", active: " + true;
int size = message.Length;
string firstByte = message[0];
bool same = "hello" == "hel" + "lo";
```

`+` concatenates strings with strings, integers, and booleans. Equality compares
contents. Length and indexing work on bytes, not Unicode code points. Native
source literals support ASCII plus `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\`, and `\"` escapes.

## Local inference

```csharp
var count = 42;
var text = "hello";
```

`var` is local type inference, not a dynamic type. It needs an initializer and is
not valid for parameters, fields, or method returns. The released compiler supports
classes, structs, enums, interfaces, and inheritance, but not generics.

Australis-first language, firmware, kernel, and native-application direction.

Hydrogen's primary purpose is to build Australis OS and native Australis
applications. Linux is the current host and application target because it makes the
compiler practical to develop and validate today. Windows and macOS hosts are
valuable future ports, but they do not set the core work order.

## Completed foundation

- Hydrogen compiles its own compiler project closure.
- The default output is direct Linux x86-64 ELF.
- The self-hosted compiler emits a PE32+ `uefi-x64` application.
- Australis packages a UEFI bootloader and raw Hylang kernel into a hybrid ISO.
- The UEFI target clears the console, waits for a key, and chain-loads an EFI image.
- The early kernel path exits boot services, initializes physical memory and
  paging, and writes to a framebuffer after firmware services end.
- OS manifests build separate bootloader and kernel images into an output tree.
- The current compiler checkout builds checked AUEX `.exec` applications from
  Hylang projects for the Australis shell.
- Australis loads bounded AUN1 machine-code children in ring 3 and contains
  their faults. This native loader is separate from Hydrogen's AUEX backend.

Linux runtime services and the constrained UEFI built-ins.

These services are implemented by the released compiler's Linux-native runtime.
The development AUEX backend also implements `Console.Write`, `WriteLine`,
`System.IO.File.Exists`, `ReadAllText`, `WriteAllText`, and
`System.Convert.ToInt32`. AUEX additionally implements `Console.ReadLine`;
its console and file text values are limited to 255 bytes. Use the fully
qualified names shown here.

| Call | Result | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `System.Console.Write(value)` | `void` | Print a string, integer, or boolean |
| `System.Console.WriteLine(value)` | `void` | Print a value followed by a newline |
| `System.IO.File.Exists(path)` | `bool` | Test a path |
| `System.IO.File.ReadAllText(path)` | `string` | Read a file as bytes in a string |
| `System.IO.File.ReadAllBytes(path)` | `byte[]` | Read a file into an array |
| `System.IO.File.WriteAllText(path, text)` | `void` | Create or replace a text file |
| `System.IO.File.WriteAllBytes(path, data)` | `void` | Create or replace a binary file |
| `System.Convert.ToInt32(text)` | `int` | Parse a signed decimal integer |

`ToInt32` returns Hydrogen's 32-bit `int`. Malformed/out-of-range values and failed
I/O terminate the application with an error. `WriteLine()` accepts no argument for
an empty line. `Console.ReadLine` is currently AUEX-only.

Managed values, the Linux-native runtime, and the UEFI target boundary.

Hydrogen programs use managed class objects, value-type structs, immutable byte
strings, and mutable arrays. Allocation and collection are automatic. Class and
array assignment copy references; struct assignment copies the value.

## Linux-native executables

The compiler embeds a Linux x86-64 runtime using raw Linux syscalls for console,
files, and memory mappings. It does not depend on libc, a C++ runtime, an assembler,
or a linker at application compilation time.

The heap uses a conservative, non-moving mark/sweep collector. Stack/register
values and heap payloads are scanned for allocation and interior pointers. Reachable
graphs and cycles are retained; unreachable mappings are reclaimed. Conservative
scanning can retain values that are no longer logically reachable.

Null access, out-of-range indices, malformed integers, failed I/O, and allocation
failure report errors and terminate with status `1`.

## UEFI output

The `uefi-x64` target has no embedded managed runtime. It emits PE32+ firmware
applications from a restricted static-entry sequence. Boot images can use UEFI
console, key-wait, and image-launch services. Kernel images can leave boot
services, establish early memory and paging, write to the GOP framebuffer, and
halt. See [UEFI Hello World and kernel handoff](/getting-started/uefi-hello/).

## Australis development formats

The current development compiler emits AUEX `.exec` images for Australis. The
kernel checks their instructions and memory accesses in its interpreter, and
provides bounded terminal, file, process, and channel calls. AUEX does not run
in hardware user mode. Separately, the OS can load small AUN1 machine-code
children in ring 3, with private user mappings and a stack guard. AUN1 currently
has PID and exit syscalls, and a fault ends only that child. Hydrogen does not
yet compile source into AUN1 or supply a managed native Australis runtime.

Build a checked AUEX .exec program from a Hylang project.

The current **development compiler checkout** can build Hylang `exec` projects
for Australis OS. This workflow is newer than the published Hydrogen
`alpha-0.0.2` release. Australis loads the resulting `.exec` file through its
checked AUEX v1 interpreter; it is not a Linux ELF or native ring-3 process.
Australis also has a separate, bounded AUN1 ring-3 loader, but Hydrogen does
not yet compile Hylang source into AUN1.

## Create and build a project

```bash
hy new exec Example
```

The format-2 manifest contains `type = "exec"`, source paths, and a plain
`.exec` output filename:

```toml
format = 2
name = "Example"
version = "0.1.0"
type = "exec"
output = "example.exec"
sources = ["Program.hy"]
project_references = []
```

An AUEX v1 entry point is `public static void Main(string[] args)` or
`public static int Main(string[] args)`. Shell arguments populate `args`.
For example:

```csharp
public class Program {
    public static int Main(string[] args) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i = i + 1) {
            total = total + i;
        }
        System.Console.WriteLine(total);
        return total;
    }
}
```

```bash
hy build Example/Example.hyproj -o example.exec
```

The source subset supports scoped scalar and string locals, assignment,
arithmetic, comparisons, short-circuit Boolean operators, `if`/`else`, `while`,
`for`, `break`, `continue`, scalar console output, and computed exit codes.
Portable source can use `System.Console.ReadLine()`,
`System.IO.File.Exists(path)`, `System.IO.File.ReadAllText(path)`,
`System.IO.File.WriteAllText(path, text)`, and
`System.Convert.ToInt32(text)`.
Returned strings remain valid across later reads; console lines and text files
are currently limited to 255 bytes. The `System.Australis.*` builtins provide
additional metadata, directory, writable-file, cooperative-yield, and low-level
operations. The current development backend also supports application method
calls, bounded strings and byte arrays, and concurrent AUEX child processes.
Native thread preemption and a general managed native Australis runtime remain
future work.

```csharp
public class Program {
    public static void Main(string[] args) {
        System.Console.Write("Name: ");
        string name = System.Console.ReadLine();
        string message = System.IO.File.ReadAllText("/hello.txt");
        System.IO.File.WriteAllText("/data/last-name.txt", name);
        System.Console.WriteLine(name);
        System.Console.Write(message);
    }
}
```

## Targets

Without `--target`, output is Linux x86-64 ELF with the native runtime.

`compile --target uefi-x64` emits a PE32+ EFI application. Its static entry
point can write ASCII literals, clear the firmware screen, wait for a key, and
launch one EFI image. A separate constrained kernel path can exit boot services,
initialize early memory, paging, heap, and framebuffer output, then halt. See
[UEFI Hello World and kernel handoff](/getting-started/uefi-hello/) for the
required call order. General-purpose firmware APIs and arbitrary method bodies
are not supported by this target.

## Errors

Commands return `0` on success and nonzero for invalid input or unsupported
compilation. A failed compilation does not create or overwrite the requested output.
An existing executable may therefore be from an earlier successful build.

Install exact source dependencies into a Hydrogen project.

The development compiler has a project-local source package manager. The
published `alpha-0.0.2` compiler does not include it yet. Packages contain a
format 2 library manifest and flat `.hy` source files. Installation runs no
package hooks or scripts.

```bash
hy package search math
hy package add App.hyproj hydrogen.math@0.1.0
hy build App.hyproj -o app
```

The first curated sample is `hydrogen.math@0.1.0`, which provides
`HydrogenMath.IntegerMath.Min`, `Max`, and `Clamp`. The registry lives at
`https://hylang.co.uk/registry/v1/`. Versions are exact; an unversioned add
does not silently select a release.

`add` writes a `[dependencies]` entry to the project, downloads its transitive
source dependencies into `.hylang/packages`, and writes `hy.lock`. Commit the
manifest and lockfile. Builds verify the package archives, manifests and source
file hashes against the lockfile.

```bash
hy package restore App.hyproj
hy package upgrade App.hyproj hydrogen.math@0.2.0
hy package remove App.hyproj hydrogen.math
```

`restore` downloads the exact archives in `hy.lock` and checks the resulting
file hashes. `upgrade` requires an explicit target version and rolls back the
project manifest and lockfile on failure. `remove` drops a direct dependency
and refreshes the lockfile; cached archive files can remain on disk.

For local development, `hy package pack Library/Library.hyproj -o Library.hypkg`
creates a source archive and `hy package add App.hyproj Library.hypkg` adds it
without using the website. The `--registry <origin>` option on search, remote
add, restore, and upgrade can point to another HTTPS registry or a `file://`
test registry. Packages submitted to the official registry are reviewed and
committed with their SHA-256 digests; there is no open upload endpoint.

Organize executable, EFI, kernel, OS, and Australis application projects.

A `.hyproj` manifest lists sources compiled together. Paths are relative to the
manifest, including referenced projects.

```text
Demo/
  App/App.hyproj
  App/Program.hy
  Math/Math.hyproj
  Math/Math.hy
```

`App/App.hyproj`:

```toml
format = 2
name = "App"
type = "exe"
sources = ["Program.hy"]
project_references = ["../Math/Math.hyproj"]
```

`Math/Math.hyproj`:

```toml
format = 2
name = "Math"
type = "lib"
sources = ["Math.hy"]
```

Build the executable project:

```bash
hy build Demo/App/App.hyproj -o Demo/app
chmod +x Demo/app
./Demo/app
```

Referenced libraries contribute sources to the final executable; they are not
separately linked artifacts.

## EFI and OS projects

Use `type = "efi"` for a boot image and `type = "kernel"` for a kernel image.
An OS manifest references those projects, and each child declares a relative
`output` path:

```toml
# OS.hyproj
format = 2
name = "Demo.OS"
type = "os"
project_references = ["Boot/Boot.hyproj", "Kernel/Kernel.hyproj"]
```

```toml
# Boot/Boot.hyproj
format = 2
name = "Demo.Boot"
type = "efi"
output = "EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI"
sources = ["program.hy"]
project_references = []
```

The kernel manifest uses `type = "kernel"` and its own output path, such as
`EFI/KERNEL.EFI`. Build both images into a directory with:

```bash
hy check OS.hyproj
hy build OS.hyproj -o image-root
```

`output` paths must stay below `image-root` and be unique. OS projects contain
references and no direct sources. Both images still use the restricted UEFI
target, described in [UEFI Hello World and kernel handoff](/getting-started/uefi-hello/).
The compiler does not package the result as a bootable ISO.

The CLI can scaffold manifests with `hy new os Demo`, `hy new efi Boot`, and
`hy new kernel Kernel`. Edit the generated manifests to add the OS references.
It does not build workspace or test projects as native outputs. The newer
development compiler has source packages, described in
[Packages and the registry](/tools/packages/); the published `alpha-0.0.2`
compiler does not include that workflow.

## Current Australis development projects

The compiler checkout used by the current Australis OS development build adds
`type = "exec"` for AUEX `.exec` applications and emits the OS kernel as a raw
`AUKR` image at `EFI/AUSTRALIS/KERNEL.BIN`. These features are newer than the documented `alpha-0.0.2`
release described above. Use a compiler checkout with this support when building
the current OS tree.

An `exec` manifest uses format 2 and a plain `.exec` output filename:

```toml
format = 2
name = "Example"
type = "exec"
output = "example.exec"
sources = ["Program.hy"]
project_references = []
```

Create one with `hy new exec Example`, or build an existing project with
`hy build Example/Example.hyproj -o example.exec`. An aggregate `os` project
can reference `exec` projects alongside the bootloader and kernel. See
[Australis applications](/tools/australis-applications/) for the supported
entry point and source features.

The current OS also accepts bounded AUN1 native images under `/System/Bin`,
but the Hydrogen `exec` backend emits AUEX, not AUN1. AUN1 is presently built
by the OS's small machine-code test-image tool.

EFI and OS projects

Section titled “EFI and OS projects”

Use type = "efi" for a boot image and type = "kernel" for a kernel image. An OS manifest references those projects, and each child declares a relative output path:

The kernel manifest uses type = "kernel" and its own output path, such as EFI/KERNEL.EFI. Build both images into a directory with:

output paths must stay below image-root and be unique. OS projects contain references and no direct sources. Both images still use the restricted UEFI target, described in UEFI Hello World and kernel handoff. The compiler does not package the result as a bootable ISO.

The CLI can scaffold manifests with hy new os Demo, hy new efi Boot, and hy new kernel Kernel. Edit the generated manifests to add the OS references. It does not build workspace or test projects as native outputs. The newer development compiler has source packages, described in Packages and the registry; the published alpha-0.0.2 compiler does not include that workflow.
